title: Clinical Fairness Handbook
text:
Welcome
A prediction model can work well on average and still let some patients down. It may miss illness more often in one group, overstate risk in another, or recommend support that patients cannot actually access. Understanding these differences takes more than a single fairness score.
This handbook is about asking useful questions, choosing appropriate measurements, and being clear about what the answers do and do not show. It is written for clinicians, researchers, ML engineers, auditors, service leads, and anyone asked to make sense of a clinical model’s performance across patient groups.
It is a companion to the Clinical Fairness Toolkit (CFT). You do not need to use CFT to read it. The clinical questions come first; software helps gather the evidence.

The questions we return to

What clinical decision will the prediction inform?
Who is represented, and who is missing?
Does the recorded outcome measure the thing we care about?
What does good performance mean for this task and this action?
Which group differences matter, and how uncertain are they?
What changes after an intervention, including downstream work and harm?

The book separates model scores, decisions, uncertainty, and patient outcomes. Keeping these separate helps prevent a promising statistical result from being mistaken for evidence that care has improved.

title: 1  Introduction and background
text:
1.1 Why this matters
Imagine a hospital using a score to offer extra support after discharge. The model has a reassuring overall performance summary. Yet one group of patients is often missed. Another is referred frequently, but finds the follow-up service difficult to reach. The model, the referral rule, and the service can each contribute to the difference.
An overall average hides how performance is distributed. A large group can dominate that average, leaving a smaller group’s poor results almost invisible. Even a model with similar error rates across groups may be unsuitable if its outcome is a poor measure of clinical need.
Clinical fairness asks how a prediction system affects different patients and whether those differences are justified. That question includes measurement, access, clinical benefit, burden, and accountability. Statistical fairness measures help examine parts of it. They do not settle the whole question (Rajkomar et al. 2018; Selbst et al. 2019).
The short CFT paper begins with a practical problem: researchers are increasingly asked to assess fairness, but assembling cohort information, task-specific metrics, subgroup comparisons, and assumptions into one report takes work. The long paper adds an important lesson: an intervention can improve the property it targets while worsening something else (McCarthy 2026b, 2026a). This handbook explains how to recognise those situations.

title: 1  Introduction and background
section: 1.2 Four things that are often called fairness
text:
1.2 Four things that are often called fairness
Representation asks whose records are available. A hospital dataset cannot directly describe people who could not access the hospital. Good balance among recorded patients does not establish good population coverage.
Predictive performance asks how well a model predicts a defined outcome. This includes discrimination, calibration, and errors. Different groups may have different performance even when the same code is applied to everyone.
Decision fairness asks how the model’s output is converted into action. A threshold, a capacity limit, or a review rule can create differences that are not apparent from the score alone.
Health equity concerns avoidable and unjust differences in opportunities, care, and health. An audit of predictions can inform that discussion. Establishing that a changed model improves health equity requires evidence about the resulting care and outcomes.
These questions connect, but their answers are not interchangeable. Equal referral rates do not prove equal benefit. Equal sensitivity does not prove that everyone had an equal chance of being diagnosed in the first place.

title: 1  Introduction and background
section: 1.3 Who benefits from reading this book?
text:
1.3 Who benefits from reading this book?
Clinicians bring knowledge of the decision, the timing of information, and the consequences of error. They can recognise when a technically convenient endpoint is clinically misleading.
Researchers need to define an evaluable question and avoid overstating what their study establishes. They also need to distinguish exploratory comparisons from a procedure evaluated on genuinely new data.
ML engineers translate the question into a reliable pipeline. Their responsibilities include keeping patients in the correct partitions, checking class order and units, preserving missing results, and making changes reproducible.
Auditors and service leads need an evidence trail. They should be able to find the population, outcome, intended action, assumptions, group definitions, limitations, and person responsible for the next decision.
Patients and public contributors help identify burdens that a model-development team might overlook. Travel, language, time away from work, fear of a procedure, and the ability to challenge a decision can matter as much as a numerical performance difference.

title: 1  Introduction and background
text:
1.4 A companion to the toolkit
CFT brings task-aware model evaluation and subgroup evidence into a shared reporting workflow. Its central role is to organise an audit of an existing model, a prediction table, or an illustrative model trained for the task. Descriptive data review can also be useful before predictions are available (McCarthy 2026b).
The book is broader than the software. It includes clinical utility, causal questions, fairness-aware training, and service monitoring even where the toolkit does not calculate the required evidence. A topic’s inclusion here is not a statement that CFT implements it.
The distinction between software checks and clinical validation matters throughout. A software test can show that a routine computes a specified metric or rejects an invalid input. It cannot show that a hospital should deploy the resulting policy.

title: 1  Introduction and background
text:
1.5 What guidance contributes
TRIPOD+AI provides reporting guidance for prediction-model studies, including attention to fairness and relevant subgroups. FUTURE-AI places fairness within the wider development and use of healthcare AI (Collins et al. 2024; Lekadir et al. 2025). These frameworks help structure questions and evidence. They do not provide one universal numerical definition of a fair clinical model.
This book therefore starts with the proposed use. It does not assign an automatic pass mark to demographic parity, equal opportunity, or any other metric.

A readmission score might be used to offer a telephone call, schedule a home visit, postpone discharge, or describe the workload expected next month. These are different uses. Their costs, benefits, and acceptable errors differ.

title: 2  Clinical applications: start with the action
text:
2.2 Rule-out: avoiding missed cases
A rule-out policy aims to identify people unlikely to have the condition or event of concern, so that further investigation can be reduced or deferred. Missing a true case is often the central concern. Sensitivity measures the proportion of actual cases detected. Negative predictive value (NPV) describes how often a negative result is correct in the evaluated population.
A high NPV can be reassuring, but it is strongly affected by prevalence. If almost nobody has the condition, a policy can have high NPV while detecting few of the people who do. A rule-out evaluation therefore needs sensitivity, missed-case counts, prevalence, follow-up, and the consequences of a false negative alongside NPV.
For example, a low-risk classification could support avoiding an immediate test. The audit should ask whether missed cases are clinically serious, whether patients can return if symptoms change, and whether that safety pathway is equally accessible. The arithmetic alone does not answer those questions.

title: 2  Clinical applications: start with the action
text:
2.3 Rule-in: avoiding unnecessary action
A rule-in policy aims to identify people for further investigation or action. Specificity measures how often people without the outcome are not flagged. Positive predictive value (PPV) describes how often flagged people have the outcome.
False positives may cause anxiety, invasive testing, medication exposure, or time-consuming appointments. They can also use capacity that would otherwise serve other patients. The importance of these burdens depends on what follows a positive result.
High specificity is not enough to establish a good rule-in tool in a low-prevalence population. Even a small false-positive rate can generate many false alarms when non-cases greatly outnumber cases.

title: 2  Clinical applications: start with the action
text:
2.5 Capacity changes the question
Suppose a service has 50 appointments each week. Lowering a threshold may improve sensitivity in validation data, but it may also create 200 referrals. The resulting policy includes a queue, a rationing rule, or a new capacity requirement. Ignoring that step leaves the clinical intervention undefined.
Capacity can affect groups differently. A first-come-first-served process may disadvantage people with inflexible work or limited access to booking systems. An apparently equal offer rate may become unequal attendance or completion.
Audit the sequence: eligible patients, offers, bookings, attendance, treatment, and outcomes. Each stage has a different denominator. Where possible, separate a patient’s informed decision to decline from barriers that make accepting difficult.

title: 2  Clinical applications: start with the action
text:
2.6 Risk and benefit are different
A model of untreated risk does not automatically identify who benefits most from treatment. Patients with the same risk can respond differently, and treatment may impose different burdens. Observational outcomes also reflect treatments patients have already received.
The CFT papers use risk and recorded outcomes to illustrate auditing. They do not estimate the causal effect of offering an intervention. A threshold policy that improves detection therefore still needs an argument about the value of acting on those detections (McCarthy 2026; Coston et al. 2020).

title: 3  Data and audit design
text:
3.1 Define the question before opening the results
An audit needs an intended population, setting, prediction time, outcome, action, and evaluation period. It also needs a named object: a score, a thresholded decision, a prediction interval, or a complete service pathway.
Write down primary comparisons in advance. Include clinically important groups and intersections, the reason for each choice, and the evidence needed to interpret a difference. Additional analyses can be valuable, but should be described as exploratory if they arise after reviewing results.
The term estimand means the quantity the analysis is trying to estimate. For example, sensitivity among eligible discharged patients with a recorded readmission within 30 days is a different estimand from sensitivity among all admissions. Both can be computed correctly while answering different questions.

title: 3  Data and audit design
text:
3.2 The outcome is a measurement
Recorded expenditure measures spending. It does not directly measure need. Recorded diagnosis depends on assessment, testing, coding, and access. Readmission depends partly on whether a patient returns to a hospital captured by the dataset.
Obermeyer and colleagues provide an influential example of a cost-based proxy producing unequal allocation relative to health need (Obermeyer et al. 2019). The general lesson is to inspect the relationship between a convenient label and the intended clinical purpose. If the target is unsuitable, changing thresholds may leave the main problem untouched.
Ask how the outcome was obtained, whether the process differs by group, and whether absence of a record means absence of the event. Differential verification is especially important: if only flagged patients receive a definitive test, observed labels can depend on the very policy being evaluated.

title: 3  Data and audit design
text:
3.3 Time belongs in the specification
Predictors must be available at the proposed prediction time. A discharge summary cannot support an admission-time prediction. A recorded follow-up duration can contain information about future events or observation and is not a baseline feature simply because it is in the same table.
The CFT papers explicitly exclude Heart Failure follow-up time from baseline predictors. They also distinguish a day-three SUPPORT landmark cohort from the full admission population (McCarthy 2026). These are teaching examples of why eligibility and timing must be stated before performance is interpreted.

“Calibration data” here is a data role. It may be used for a threshold, transport map, or conformal residuals; it does not necessarily mean fitting a probability calibrator.
Repeatedly inspecting a test set and choosing the most attractive intervention turns that set into development data. A new independent evaluation is then needed. Recording random seeds is useful for reproducibility, but does not undo that reuse.

title: 3  Data and audit design
text:
3.5 Keep related records together
Repeated encounters from the same patient should stay in one partition when the intended evaluation concerns new patients. Household-linked expenditure records should also be grouped. Otherwise, shared information can make performance look better than it will be on new independent units.
The appropriate split depends on the deployment question. A temporal split can study a later period. A hospital-held-out split can study transfer to a new site. Neither automatically solves leakage if records cross boundaries or preprocessing uses the whole dataset.
For uncertainty estimates, the resampling unit should match dependence in the data. Resampling encounter rows independently is usually inappropriate when outcomes within a patient are correlated. Survey data may additionally require design weights, strata, and primary sampling units.

title: 3  Data and audit design
section: 3.6 Audit attributes are not ordinary columns
text:
3.6 Audit attributes are not ordinary columns
Document what each attribute records, who assigned it, when it was collected, and how missing values arise. Sex, gender, race, ethnicity, language, disability, and deprivation are not interchangeable concepts. Administrative categories are often incomplete descriptions of a person’s circumstances.
Do not infer that removing a sensitive attribute from predictors removes all related information. Other fields can act as proxies. Conversely, deciding whether a variable should be used in prediction is a separate question from whether it should be retained for audit (Gichoya et al. 2022; Vyas et al. 2020).
For this handbook’s baseline examples, audit fields are kept separate from predictors. A group-aware postprocessor may still need the group at deployment. That requirement must be explicit.
Keep an accounting of unknown and missing group values. If a method cannot handle them, report the resulting exclusion and the population to which results apply. Do not silently fold a collection of different groups into a single category to satisfy a two-group method.

title: 3  Data and audit design
text:
3.7 Missingness and selection
Missing predictors can reflect different access to testing. A missingness indicator may be predictive precisely because care differs. Imputation should be fitted on training data, and its effects should be examined across groups. A technically successful imputation does not establish that the measurement process is equitable.
Missing outcomes are more serious than a blank input field. If follow-up is incomplete, a complete-case audit may describe only those who remain observed. Compare available characteristics of included and excluded patients and explain why the missing-outcome mechanism is plausible or uncertain.
Privacy also affects reporting. Small cells may create disclosure risks, but suppressing them in a public report should not be presented as evidence that no disparity exists. Document the reporting rule and preserve appropriate internal review where authorised.

title: 4  Modelling approaches
text:
4.1 Choose the task from the question
The outcome determines the task. A binary model answers a two-category question. A multiclass model selects among mutually exclusive categories. Regression predicts a numeric quantity. Survival analysis addresses event timing with incomplete follow-up.
These tasks can describe related clinical topics without answering the same question. Predicting a death flag from variable follow-up is not equivalent to predicting the probability of death within six months. Turning expenditure into “high” or “low” discards information and introduces a threshold that needs justification.
These are the model families used to illustrate CFT workflows. The book does not depend on deep learning. A sophisticated model family does not remove the need to specify data roles, timing, and outcome meaning (McCarthy 2026b, 2026a).

title: 4  Modelling approaches
text:
4.2 Binary classification
Let \(S=f(X)\) be a score estimating \(P(Y=1\mid X)\). A threshold \(t\) produces a decision
\[
D=\mathbf{1}\{S\ge t\}.
\]
The positive class must be named. It could be readmission, disease, or eligibility for support. The label “positive” does not mean beneficial. Scores and decisions require different evaluation: a threshold can change sensitivity without changing the underlying ranking.
Logistic regression models log-odds as a function of predictors. Tree ensembles can capture nonlinear relationships and interactions. Either can be poorly calibrated or fail in a new population. Model family is not a substitute for evaluation.

title: 4  Modelling approaches
text:
4.3 Multiclass classification
A multiclass predictor returns \(p(x)=(p_1,\ldots,p_K)\), with \(p_k\ge0\) and \(\sum_kp_k=1\). A common decision is \(\arg\max_k p_k\).
Readmission recorded as none, within 30 days, or later is one example. The categories preserve information that a binary endpoint would collapse. They also introduce class-specific questions: a high overall accuracy may be driven by the common “none” class while the clinically important early-readmission class is rarely detected.
One-versus-rest metrics are useful summaries. However, applying a separate threshold to every class can return several classes or no class. A mutually exclusive task needs a joint decision rule.
Multiclass is also different from multilabel prediction, where several conditions can coexist. Ordinal categories, such as ordered disease stages, add a structure that ordinary multiclass methods may ignore. State these distinctions before interpreting errors.

title: 4  Modelling approaches
text:
4.4 Regression
A regression model predicts a numeric quantity in defined units. Examples include expenditure, a disease-progression score, or length of stay. An error of 10 means something very different in pounds, days, or a laboratory scale.
Ridge regression provides a regularised linear reference. Boosted trees allow nonlinear relationships. A Tweedie model with a suitable link can be useful for some nonnegative, zero-heavy outcomes. The distribution and intended use should guide the choice.
For skewed outcomes, mean error can be dominated by a small upper tail. A logarithmic transformation changes the fitting target. Exponentiating a prediction of the mean log outcome generally does not recover the mean outcome on the original scale. Evaluate on the scale required by the clinical or service question, with any retransformation described.

title: 4  Modelling approaches
text:
4.5 Survival analysis
Let \(T\) be the event time and \(C\) the censoring time. We observe
\[
U=\min(T,C),\qquad \delta=\mathbf{1}\{T\le C\}.
\]
If a person is last seen at day 40 without the event, their day-90 outcome is unknown. Coding them as a permanent non-event gives the wrong target.
A survival curve is \(S(t\mid X)=P(T>t\mid X)\). The event risk by horizon \(\tau\) is \(1-S(\tau\mid X)\). A curve must stay between zero and one and cannot increase with time.
The Cox model expresses a hazard as \(h(t\mid X)=h_0(t)\exp(X^\top\beta)\) and assumes proportional hazards in its usual form (Cox 1972). Its linear predictor gives a risk ordering; probabilities also need the baseline hazard. Random survival forests provide a tree-based alternative (Ishwaran et al. 2008). Their outputs still need censoring-aware evaluation.
The origin of time is essential. Survival from admission, from diagnosis, or from a day-three landmark concerns different populations. A landmark analysis includes people who meet the eligibility conditions at that landmark; its results should not be applied as if they described everyone at admission.
Competing events, recurrent events, and time-varying predictors require additional methods. For example, death can prevent a later readmission. Treating a competing event as ordinary censoring does not generally estimate the cumulative incidence of the event of interest. This handbook’s CFT examples concern a stated single-event, right-censored task, not a general solution to these extensions (Fine and Gray 1999).

title: 5  Utility: is the prediction useful?
text:
5.1 Start with counts and consequences
Clinical utility concerns the value and burden of using a prediction. Performance metrics describe parts of that question. They are easiest to interpret when the underlying counts and proposed action remain visible (Steyerberg et al. 2010).
For a binary task, true positives (TP) are detected cases, false negatives (FN) are missed cases, false positives (FP) are flagged non-cases, and true negatives (TN) are unflagged non-cases.
A zero denominator means the rate is undefined. If no patients are flagged, PPV is not zero; it cannot be estimated from that group. If there are no observed cases, sensitivity is undefined. Keep that distinction visible.
Accuracy weights errors according to their frequency in the dataset. Balanced accuracy gives the two true outcome classes equal weight. Neither automatically reflects clinical consequences. F1 combines precision and recall but leaves true negatives out of its formula; it is not a universal clinical utility measure.

\((\mathrm{TPR}+\mathrm{TNR})/2\)
How well are the two outcome classes detected on average?
crumbs: 5  Utility: is the prediction useful?

title: 5  Utility: is the prediction useful?
text:
5.2 Discrimination: ordering patients
AUROC summarises how well scores rank cases above non-cases, with an appropriate convention for ties. It does not specify a threshold or quantify the usefulness of acting on a prediction.
Precision-recall summaries focus on detection among positive predictions and can be informative for uncommon outcomes. Average precision depends on prevalence, so comparisons across populations need care. A good ranking can coexist with inaccurate absolute risks.
For a decision-only postprocessor, source-score AUROC may be unchanged even when the decisions change. That is expected: it measures a different object.
crumbs: 5  Utility: is the prediction useful?

title: 5  Utility: is the prediction useful?
section: 5.3 Calibration: the meaning of a probability
text:
5.3 Calibration: the meaning of a probability
A calibrated risk of 20% means that, among comparable predictions near 20%, the observed event frequency is about 20% in the stated population and time frame. Formally, ideal group calibration is
\[
E[Y\mid S=s,A=a]=s.
\]
In practice, exact score values may have few observations. Calibration plots use smoothing or bins, with enough data to support interpretation. Report group support and uncertainty; a smooth line can conceal sparse regions.
Calibration-in-the-large examines average over- or underprediction. A calibration slope can reveal predictions that are too extreme or insufficiently spread out. A full calibration curve can reveal local errors that these summaries miss (Topic Group ’Evaluating diagnostic tests et al. 2019).
The Brier score is
\[
\operatorname{BS}=\frac1n\sum_i(S_i-Y_i)^2.
\]
It is a probability-error score, influenced by more than calibration alone. Log loss also evaluates probabilities and strongly penalises confident mistakes. Calling either a pure “calibration metric” obscures that distinction.

Illustration placeholder — A risk label that means what it says.
Show three reliability curves: close to the diagonal, systematic overprediction, and different group curves hidden by an acceptable pooled curve. Include a rug or count strip below the plots. Use schematic data and explicitly label the diagonal as ideal calibration.
crumbs: 5  Utility: is the prediction useful?

title: 5  Utility: is the prediction useful?
text:
5.4 From prediction to net benefit
Decision-curve analysis links a binary decision to a threshold probability \(p_t\), under a specified relative value of false positives and true positives. A common net-benefit expression is
\[
\operatorname{NB}(p_t)=\frac{TP}{n}-\frac{FP}{n}\frac{p_t}{1-p_t}.
\]
The weighting expresses how much harm from an unnecessary action is accepted relative to benefit from an appropriate one. Compare the model policy with relevant alternatives, often acting on everyone or no one (Vickers and Elkin 2006).
This is a decision model, not observed treatment benefit. Its interpretation needs a suitable endpoint, a credible action, and meaningful threshold preferences. A subgroup net-benefit curve may be useful, but it does not make waiting time, access, or all patient burdens disappear. Decision curves are covered here as an evaluation concept; this book does not claim that CFT automatically supplies them.
crumbs: 5  Utility: is the prediction useful?

title: 5  Utility: is the prediction useful?
text:
5.5 Utility across the other tasks
For multiclass prediction, report the confusion matrix and each class’s detection and predictive value. Macro averages give classes equal weight; weighted averages can be dominated by common classes. Multiclass log loss and Brier scores use the full probability vector. If some mistakes are more serious, define a cost matrix \(L_{yk}\) for predicting class \(k\) when the true class is \(y\).
For regression, define residuals here as \(e_i=\widehat Y_i-Y_i\), so positive bias means overprediction. Then
\[
\operatorname{MAE}=\frac1n\sum_i|e_i|,\quad
\operatorname{RMSE}=\sqrt{\frac1n\sum_i e_i^2},\quad
\operatorname{Bias}=\frac1n\sum_i e_i.
\]
Signed errors can cancel. RMSE emphasises large errors more strongly than MAE. Report units, group-specific errors, and clinically important tails. \(R^2\) can be negative on evaluation data and is undefined when the evaluated outcome has zero variation. It is not a direct measure of whether errors are acceptable.
For survival, concordance assesses ranking among appropriately comparable observations. Horizon AUC, Brier scores, and calibration answer time-specific questions and require censoring-aware estimators. A model can rank patients reasonably while assigning poor six-month probabilities. The censoring assumptions and supported horizons belong beside the numbers; Chapter 11 gives a worked loss formula.

title: 5  Utility: is the prediction useful?
text:
5.6 Questions to discuss

If everyone receives the same well-calibrated risk, what useful information might still be missing?
Two regression groups have zero mean signed error. Does that establish equal predictive performance?
Why should a high AUROC not be used as evidence that a referral threshold is clinically worthwhile?

title: 6  Fairness: what should be compared?
text:
6.1 Notation in plain language
Let \(A\) identify an audit group, \(Y\) the recorded outcome, \(S\) the model score, and \(D\) the decision. For now, \(Y\) and \(D\) are binary. \(D=1\) means the action is selected; it does not tell us whether that action is beneficial.
The three criteria below compare decisions. Score calibration concerns a different object. Confusing the two can lead to a report in which a change is credited to the wrong part of the system.
crumbs: 6  Fairness: what should be compared?

title: 6  Fairness: what should be compared?
text:
6.2 Demographic parity: equal selection
Demographic parity (DP) requires
\[
P(D=1\mid A=a)=P(D=1\mid A=b)
\]
for the groups being compared. A common summary is the range of selection rates:
\[
\Delta_{\mathrm{DP}}=\max_a\operatorname{SR}_a-\min_a\operatorname{SR}_a.
\]
This asks whether the same proportion of each group receives the positive decision. It can be measured without outcome labels if decisions and group membership are available.
Equal access to a scarce opportunity may motivate a selection comparison. However, equal referral fractions may be inappropriate when clinical needs differ. Conversely, a measured need difference may partly reflect unequal diagnosis or access. The clinical argument has to address both possibilities.
crumbs: 6  Fairness: what should be compared?

title: 6  Fairness: what should be compared?
section: 6.3 Equal opportunity: equal detection among cases
text:
6.3 Equal opportunity: equal detection among cases
Equal opportunity (EOpp) requires equal true-positive rates:
\[
P(D=1\mid Y=1,A=a)=P(D=1\mid Y=1,A=b),
\]
with
\[
\Delta_{\mathrm{EOpp}}=\max_a\operatorname{TPR}_a-\min_a\operatorname{TPR}_a.
\]
If a positive decision offers useful support, EOpp asks whether patients who experience the recorded outcome are detected equally often. It needs labels and enough observed cases in each group (Hardt et al. 2016).
The word “opportunity” can mislead in a clinical setting. The criterion conditions on a recorded outcome, not an observed right to care or an individual treatment benefit. Biased labels can undermine its interpretation.
Equal sensitivity of 5% gives a zero gap while missing almost all cases. Always report the group rates, counts, and direction of change alongside the gap.
crumbs: 6  Fairness: what should be compared?

title: 6  Fairness: what should be compared?
section: 6.4 Equalized odds: equal detection and false alarms
text:
6.4 Equalized odds: equal detection and false alarms
Equalized odds (EOdds) requires the decision to be independent of group conditional on the outcome:
\[
D\perp A\mid Y.
\]
For a binary outcome, this means equal TPR and equal false-positive rate (FPR). One explicit summary convention is
\[
\Delta_{\mathrm{EOdds}}=
\max\left\{\max_a\mathrm{TPR}_a-\min_a\mathrm{TPR}_a,
\max_a\mathrm{FPR}_a-\min_a\mathrm{FPR}_a\right\}.
\]
Other software may average differences or use a different pairwise comparison. State the formula rather than relying on an abbreviation. EOdds addresses both missed cases and false alarms, but still does not encode their clinical costs or the acceptability of the overall operating point (Hardt et al. 2016).
crumbs: 6  Fairness: what should be compared?

text:
6.5 Why the criteria can disagree
Consider invented groups with identical TPR of 90% and FPR of 10%, but prevalence of 20% in group A and 10% in group B.

EOdds holds in these counts. DP does not: selection differs by eight percentage points. PPV also differs.
The relationship is visible in Bayes’ rule. With prevalence \(\pi_a=P(Y=1\mid A=a)\),
\[
\mathrm{PPV}_a=
\frac{\mathrm{TPR}_a\pi_a}
{\mathrm{TPR}_a\pi_a+\mathrm{FPR}_a(1-\pi_a)}.
\]
Equal error rates therefore need not give equal predictive values when prevalence differs. The broader incompatibility literature shows that several desirable parity and calibration properties cannot generally hold together except in special cases. This is a reason to explain choices, not a reason to stop auditing (Chouldechova 2017; Kleinberg et al. 2017; Pleiss et al. 2017).

title: 6  Fairness: what should be compared?
section: 6.6 Calibration, individual fairness, and causal fairness
text:
6.6 Calibration, individual fairness, and causal fairness
Group calibration asks whether the same reported probability has the same outcome meaning within groups. It is especially relevant when patients and clinicians use probabilities directly.
Individual fairness asks whether people who are similar in relevant respects receive similar treatment. It needs a justified definition of similarity; a distance computed from convenient columns is not automatically clinically meaningful (Dwork et al. 2012).
Counterfactual fairness asks about a person’s prediction under a specified causal change to a sensitive attribute. It needs a causal model and assumptions, not just a spreadsheet edit. These ideas broaden the discussion beyond group rates and are developed in Chapter 12.
crumbs: 6  Fairness: what should be compared?

title: 6  Fairness: what should be compared?
section: 6.7 More than one group at a time
text:
6.7 More than one group at a time
Audit groups may overlap. Sex and age comparisons can each appear acceptable while an intersection performs poorly. Examine clinically justified intersections and retain their support counts. Do not claim protection for every hidden group after testing only a few broad categories (Kearns et al. 2018).
A range gap also loses direction: it does not tell the reader which group has which rate. Differences in percentage points and ratios answer different questions; ratios can become unstable near zero. Present group estimates first, then summaries.
crumbs: 6  Fairness: what should be compared?

title: 6  Fairness: what should be compared?
text:
6.8 Keep the task semantics
For multiclass tasks, DP can concern each output class’s frequency. EOpp can compare detection of each true class. Full conditional-confusion parity compares every output distribution within each true class. This is stronger than a few one-versus-rest summaries.
For regression, compare signed error, error magnitude, relevant tail behaviour, prediction distributions, or interval coverage according to the question. Binary TPR and FPR are not generic regression errors. Defining a clinical event from a continuous outcome creates a new threshold-specific question.
For survival, a binary comparison at horizon \(\tau\) concerns \(\mathbf{1}\{T\le\tau\}\). That label is unknown for patients censored before \(\tau\) and requires appropriate methods. Comparing raw event flags across unequal follow-up does not answer the horizon question.

Illustration placeholder — Three denominators.
For DP, highlight everyone. For EOpp, highlight actual cases. For EOdds, show separate case and non-case panels. Draw selected patients within each denominator. Use direct labels as well as colour.

In the invented table, why does PPV differ despite equalized odds?

title: 7  Uncertainty, small groups, and interpretation
text:
7.1 A rate is an estimate
Suppose a model detects nine of ten cases in one group and 900 of 1,000 in another. Both sensitivities are 90%. The first is much less precisely estimated. Group size alone is not enough: sensitivity depends on the number of cases, specificity on non-cases, and PPV on positive decisions.
As a rough illustration, the independent-binomial standard error is \(\sqrt{\widehat p(1-\widehat p)/n}\). It is not a good default interval method for very small counts or extreme rates. Suitable binomial intervals, resampling, or a justified model can better represent uncertainty. Dependence and weighting can require further changes.
Do not turn unsupported rates into zeros. “Not estimable: no observed cases” is an informative result. “No evidence of a difference” also does not mean the groups are equivalent. To support a claim of practically similar performance, define a meaningful margin and assess whether the evidence is precise enough for that claim.
crumbs: 7  Uncertainty, small groups, and interpretation

title: 7  Uncertainty, small groups, and interpretation
section: 7.2 Plan for the smallest important denominator
text:
7.2 Plan for the smallest important denominator
A large dataset may contain very few events in a clinically important intersection. Planning should consider the quantities that matter: group events, non-events, selected cases, observed follow-up, or independent clusters.
There is no universal minimum group size that makes all metrics reliable. Precision depends on the rate, the comparison, the sampling design, and the consequences of uncertainty. An implementation’s minimum count is a software rule, not a clinical assurance threshold.
If evidence is too sparse, useful responses include additional data collection, a narrower claim, or a study design that deliberately improves representation. Combining groups solely to make a result look stable may erase the people whose experience prompted the audit.
crumbs: 7  Uncertainty, small groups, and interpretation

title: 7  Uncertainty, small groups, and interpretation
text:
7.3 Uncertainty in a difference
Report intervals for the quantity you intend to discuss. Intervals for two group rates are not an interval for their difference. Likewise, a bootstrap interval for a selected maximum-minus-minimum gap involves a data-dependent summary; describe exactly what was resampled and recalculated.
Paired intervention comparisons should preserve the pairing: each resampled patient contributes both baseline and adjusted predictions. This helps distinguish a policy change from differences in the evaluated sample.
Resample patients for correlated encounters, households for relevant household-linked data, and appropriate units for clustered site designs. A survey-weighted point estimate does not automatically have a valid survey-design interval. Group sample sizes and design effects can matter as much as the total number of rows.
crumbs: 7  Uncertainty, small groups, and interpretation

title: 7  Uncertainty, small groups, and interpretation
text:
7.4 What the interval conditions on
Resampling a fixed evaluation dataset with a fixed model estimates uncertainty conditional on that fitted procedure and the sampling assumptions. It does not capture every source of model-training variation, threshold-selection variation, or future distribution shift.
If the question concerns the whole learning procedure, resampling or repeated validation may need to repeat fitting and selection without leaking evaluation outcomes. That is a larger and more expensive question. State which uncertainty has actually been estimated.
The long CFT paper reports variation across seeded splits but explicitly does not treat it as external-performance confidence intervals. The same patients can appear across seeds, so those runs are not independent replications (McCarthy 2026).
crumbs: 7  Uncertainty, small groups, and interpretation

title: 7  Uncertainty, small groups, and interpretation
text:
7.5 Many comparisons invite attractive accidents
An audit may examine many groups, metrics, thresholds, and interventions. With enough comparisons, some striking results occur by chance. Prespecify key questions, label exploratory results, and use an appropriate multiplicity strategy where formal inference is intended.
A dashboard should still make exploratory harms visible. The goal is to avoid presenting a selected favourable comparison as if it were the only planned analysis. Clinical importance and statistical significance are different: a precisely estimated tiny gap can be unimportant, while an uncertain large gap may justify collecting better evidence.

title: 8  Post-hoc methods: binary decisions and scores
text:
8.1 What “post-hoc” means
A post-hoc method keeps the base predictor fixed and changes how its output is used. The new component may still need fitting, labelled data, group information, and tuning. “Model agnostic” does not mean assumption-free or data-free.
The fitted system now includes the original predictor and the postprocessor. Fit the latter on separate development or calibration data, freeze its settings, and evaluate the whole procedure on held-out data. Preserve an unchanged baseline.
Before choosing a method, ask whether the problem is the label, score meaning, operating threshold, or downstream pathway. A threshold cannot repair an unsuitable target. Calibration cannot create a service that patients can access.

title: 8  Post-hoc methods: binary decisions and scores
text:
8.2 Group-specific thresholds
For group \(a\), a threshold \(t_a\) gives
\[
D(s,a)=\mathbf{1}\{s\ge t_a\}.
\tag{8.1}\]
Changing \(t_a\) moves the operating point. Lowering it normally increases both sensitivity and false-positive rate. A DP rule can target similar selection rates; an EOpp rule can target similar sensitivity.
A general empirical search is
\[
\min_{\{t_a\}}\widehat L(D,Y)
\quad\text{subject to}\quad
\widehat\Delta(D)\le\epsilon,
\qquad \widehat{\mathrm{TPR}}_a\ge c_a.
\tag{8.2}\]
Here \(\widehat L\) is a stated validation loss, \(\epsilon\) an allowed disparity, and \(c_a\) a sensitivity floor. This is a schematic optimisation problem, not a claim that every threshold helper solves it. Losses, grids, tie rules, and constraints differ between implementations (Hardt et al. 2016; McCarthy 2026).
CFT’s native EOpp and sensitivity helpers are documented heuristics. Its specificity, PPV, and NPV helpers search supported validation thresholds under their stated target and objective. The long paper warns that different reference operating points can produce very different clinical behaviour. A method name alone does not define an equivalent comparison.
An empirical floor is a fitted target. It can be infeasible, imprecise, or violated in another population. A PPV constraint needs enough positive decisions; an NPV constraint needs enough negative decisions. An all-negative policy cannot demonstrate PPV, and an all-positive policy cannot demonstrate NPV.
Clinical reading. If sensitivity improves from 60% to 80% in one group, also report new false positives, workload, predictive values, and uncertainty. If the gap shrinks because another group’s sensitivity falls, say so plainly.
crumbs: 8  Post-hoc methods: binary decisions and scores

title: 8  Post-hoc methods: binary decisions and scores
text:
8.3 Randomized equalized odds
Sometimes deterministic thresholds cannot reach the same TPR and FPR in different groups. Randomization can mix operating rules. A simple two-threshold illustration is
\[
q_a(s)=\lambda_a\mathbf{1}\{s\ge t_{a,1}\}
+(1-\lambda_a)\mathbf{1}\{s\ge t_{a,2}\},
\qquad D\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(q_a(s)).
\tag{8.3}\]
The fitted \(q_a\) is the probability of making a positive decision. It is not a disease probability. More general implementations can include constant or flipped rules. Hardt and colleagues develop the ROC-based post-processing construction (Hardt et al. 2016).
Fairlearn and AIF360 provide related implementations with different interfaces and choices (Weerts et al. 2023; Bellamy et al. 2018). Inspect their objective and supported groups. CFT’s strict external adapters retain incompatibility and missing-dependency states instead of claiming success through a substitute method.
Expected policy rates and realised rates in a finite sample can differ because of randomization. Record seeds for reproducibility, but also evaluate whether the clinical action can reasonably be randomized. Identical input on repeated encounters should not accidentally trigger a changing care pathway without an explicit policy.

Illustration placeholder — A point between operating rules.
Show two group ROC curves, two thresholds on one curve, and the mixture point between them. Label the axes FPR and TPR. Explain that the line segment describes expected randomized decisions, not a new calibrated risk score.

title: 8  Post-hoc methods: binary decisions and scores
text:
8.4 Recalibration
Recalibration aims to improve the meaning of a risk score. A logistic recalibration model can take the form
\[
\widetilde s=\operatorname{logit}^{-1}
\{\beta_0+\beta_1\operatorname{logit}(s)\}.
\tag{8.4}\]
The intercept adjusts overall over- or underprediction; the slope adjusts the spread. Exact zero and one scores require an explicitly documented treatment. Isotonic regression instead fits a nondecreasing relationship with fewer shape assumptions, but can be unstable with limited data.
Recalibration uses held-out labels. Group-specific versions also need sufficient group support and group membership at use time. They can change cross-group ordering and the decisions produced by a fixed threshold (Topic Group ’Evaluating diagnostic tests et al. 2019).
Ordinary recalibration is explained here as a general method. It should not be confused with CFT’s calibrated equalized-odds adapter, which has a different objective and mechanism.
crumbs: 8  Post-hoc methods: binary decisions and scores

title: 8  Post-hoc methods: binary decisions and scores
text:
8.5 Calibrated equalized-odds post-processing
Pleiss and colleagues study tensions between calibration and error-cost constraints. A conceptual adjustment mixes a source score with its group’s prevalence:
\[
\widetilde S=(1-B_a)S+B_a\pi_a,
\qquad B_a\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(\lambda_a),
\quad \pi_a=P(Y=1\mid A=a).
\tag{8.5}\]
Some predictions become less informative by being replaced with a group-level constant. The calibration-preservation argument depends on appropriately calibrated source scores and the stated randomization. The method does not generally promise simultaneous unrestricted equalized odds, calibration, and unchanged informativeness (Pleiss et al. 2017).
The CFT adapter requires explicit two-group roles and checks fitted mixture probabilities. A failed assumption or invalid fitted mixture should remain visible. A model called “logistic regression” is not evidence that its probabilities are sufficiently calibrated for the argument.
crumbs: 8  Post-hoc methods: binary decisions and scores

title: 8  Post-hoc methods: binary decisions and scores
text:
8.6 Multiaccuracy and multicalibration
Multiaccuracy looks for systematic residual error across a specified family of subpopulations or auditor functions. For a bounded auditor \(h\), a population target can be expressed as
\[
\left|E[h(X)\{Y-\widetilde S(X)\}]\right|\le\epsilon.
\]
Multicalibration adds conditions within score regions of supported subpopulations. A simplified cell-based target is
\[
\left|E[Y-\widetilde S\mid X\in G,\widetilde S\in B]\right|\le\epsilon
\]
for eligible groups \(G\) and score bins \(B\). Iterative corrections can address errors that broad averages hide. The actual guarantees depend on the auditor class, sampling, tolerances, and support (Kim et al. 2019; Hebert-Johnson et al. 2018). These equations explain research targets; they are not a guarantee that every hidden intersection is protected. CFT’s restricted survival adaptation is discussed separately in Chapter 11.
crumbs: 8  Post-hoc methods: binary decisions and scores

title: 8  Post-hoc methods: binary decisions and scores
section: 8.7 Reject options are not the same as deferral
text:
8.7 Reject options are not the same as deferral
Reject-option classification may change decisions near a decision boundary in favour of one specified group and against another to address a chosen disparity. A schematic boundary region is \(|s-t|\le m\), within which a group-dependent override is applied. The precise rule and optimisation must be stated (Kamiran et al. 2012).
Despite the name, this need not send anyone to a human reviewer. It can directly issue a changed class decision. CFT’s AIF360 wrapper follows a configured reject-option policy; it should not be described as a measured benefit from human review.
crumbs: 8  Post-hoc methods: binary decisions and scores

title: 8  Post-hoc methods: binary decisions and scores
text:
8.8 Selective prediction and deferral
A selective predictor withholds its automated decision for some patients. Let \(Q=1\) mean retained for automation and \(Q=0\) mean deferred. A simple uncertainty signal is proximity to a threshold, \(u(s)=-|s-t|\), where larger values indicate greater proximity. A cutoff \(c\) gives
\[
Q=\mathbf{1}\{u(S)\le c\}.
\]
Fit \(c\) on calibration data for a desired retained fraction and freeze it. Ties and population changes mean the achieved evaluation fraction can differ.
For group \(a\), report both
\[
\operatorname{Coverage}_a=P(Q=1\mid A=a),\qquad
R_a^{\mathrm{ret}}=E[\ell(Y,D)\mid Q=1,A=a].
\tag{8.6}\]
Retained accuracy often improves when difficult cases are removed. That does not establish better outcomes for deferred patients. A group could receive fewer automated decisions and face longer waits for review. Selective classification can also magnify group disparities (Jones et al. 2021).
Learning to defer goes further by modelling interaction with a reviewer or expert. It needs evidence about that decision-maker and cannot be inferred from a simple coverage rule (Madras et al. 2018; Mozannar and Sontag 2020).

title: 9  Post-hoc methods: multiclass decisions
text:
9.1 Keep one coherent decision
For \(K\) mutually exclusive classes, the adjusted output must still represent a joint decision. Let \(p_i\) be the source class probabilities and \(q_i\) an adjusted distribution in the simplex
\[
\Delta_K=\{q:q_k\ge0,\ \sum_kq_k=1\}.
\]
If \(q_i\) is used to sample a decision, it is a policy distribution. It should not automatically be shown to patients as a calibrated diagnostic probability. Taking its argmax creates a different policy and can change a constraint fitted for randomized decisions.

title: 9  Post-hoc methods: multiclass decisions
text:
9.2 Stochastic class transitions
Putzel and Lee describe post-processing through group-specific class-transition matrices (Putzel and Lee 2022). Let
\[
C^{(a)}_{yj}=P(\widehat Y=j\mid Y=y,A=a)
\]
be the source model’s conditional confusion matrix. Define
\[
M^{(a)}_{jk}=P(D=k\mid\widehat Y=j,A=a),\qquad
M^{(a)}_{jk}\ge0,\quad \sum_kM^{(a)}_{jk}=1.
\]
The resulting conditional confusion matrix is
\[
\widetilde C^{(a)}=C^{(a)}M^{(a)}.
\tag{9.1}\]
Each row of \(M\) describes how an original class is redistributed. For example, a row \((0.8,0.2,0)\) means an original class-1 decision stays class 1 with probability 0.8 and changes to class 2 with probability 0.2. These are invented policy values, not clinical recommendations.
A linear program can maximise empirical expected accuracy while constraining output frequencies, class detection rates, or the full conditional confusion matrix. It needs supported class-by-group cells for the constraints being estimated. An absent true class in one group cannot supply an observed conditional rate.
Equal full conditional-confusion rows are not identical to equal one-versus-rest FPRs. For class \(k\), the “rest” combines several true classes; different mixtures of those classes across groups can produce different aggregated rates.
CFT scope. The native transition implementation fits on calibration data, retains the joint randomized rule, and records unsupported cells and unseen groups. Its empirical objective does not encode arbitrary clinical misclassification costs (McCarthy 2026).

title: 9  Post-hoc methods: multiclass decisions
section: 9.3 Information projection: change probabilities as little as possible
text:
9.3 Information projection: change probabilities as little as possible
FairProjection seeks an adjusted distribution close to a base distribution while meeting fairness constraints (Alghamdi et al. 2022). An illustrative weighted empirical form is
\[
\min_{q_i\in\Delta_K}\sum_i w_i\sum_k q_{ik}\log\frac{q_{ik}}{\bar p_{ik}}
\quad\text{subject to}\quad
\left|\sum_iw_i\sum_kq_{ik}\phi_{rk}(p_i,A_i)\right|\le\epsilon_r.
\tag{9.2}\]
Here \(w_i\) are nonnegative normalised weights, \(\bar p\) is a specified smoothed source vector, and \(\phi_r\) encodes a contrast between groups. The objective is a Kullback–Leibler divergence. Its direction matters; reversing the arguments is a different objective.
For suitable linear constraints, the adjustment takes an exponential form with fitted signed multipliers \(\lambda_r\):
\[
q_k(p,a)=\frac{\bar p_k\exp\{-\sum_r\lambda_r\phi_{rk}(p,a)\}}
{\sum_l\bar p_l\exp\{-\sum_r\lambda_r\phi_{rl}(p,a)\}}.
\]
This preserves a joint distribution. “Close” is measured by the chosen divergence; it does not mean clinically inconsequential.
CFT scope. The native implementation uses a SciPy optimisation adaptation. Its conditional-error variants use source probabilities as outcome proxies in moment constraints. For example,
\[
\widehat\mu^{(a)}_{yk}(q)=
\frac{\sum_{i:A_i=a}w_i p_{iy}q_{ik}}
{\sum_{i:A_i=a}w_i p_{iy}}.
\]
This is not automatically the observed rate \(P(D=k\mid Y=y,A=a)\). If the source probabilities do not represent the required conditional outcomes, the proxy can be misleading. The implementation requires acknowledgement of the relevant calibration assumption; an acknowledgement records an assumption rather than proving it (McCarthy 2026).

title: 9  Post-hoc methods: multiclass decisions
text:
9.4 Optimal transport and LinearPost
Multiclass DP can also be framed through optimal transport. Xian and colleagues connect fair classification with a transport problem and derive post-processing results under stated assumptions on the source predictor (Xian et al. 2023). LinearPost extends the use of linear fairness constraints (Xian and Zhao 2024).
For unit misclassification cost and source probabilities \(p_{ik}\), a schematic program is
\[
\min_{q_i\in\Delta_K}\sum_iw_i\sum_k(1-p_{ik})q_{ik}
\quad\text{subject to declared group-moment bounds}.
\tag{9.3}\]
A corresponding adjusted-risk rule has the form
\[
D(p,a)=\arg\min_k\left\{1-p_k+\sum_r\lambda_r\phi_{rk}(p,a)\right\}.
\]
Finite-sample fitting, ties, and constraint feasibility need inspection. Guarantees based on ideal conditional probabilities do not transfer merely because a software model returns a vector summing to one.
CFT scope. The native adapters use attribute-aware inputs and an empirical calibration program. OT-DP and LinearPost-DP share the same empirical program in the inspected implementation; their different literature labels are not independent algorithmic evidence. A general class-cost matrix and an attribute-blind auxiliary group predictor are not supplied by that adapter (McCarthy 2026).

title: 9  Post-hoc methods: multiclass decisions
text:
9.5 Use a matched comparator
Suppose a source model predicts \((0.6,0.3,0.1)\). Argmax always chooses class 1. Sampling from the unadjusted vector chooses class 1 only 60% of the time in expectation. A randomized fairness policy compared only with argmax can therefore look different even before any fairness adjustment matters.
The long CFT paper used an additional unadjusted sampling diagnostic to expose this issue. That diagnostic was added during results review and is labelled as such. The lesson is to compare matched decision semantics and distinguish planned analyses from later investigation (McCarthy 2026).

title: 10  Post-hoc methods: regression and uncertainty intervals
text:
10.1 Three different goals
A regression audit may ask whether a model systematically underpredicts in one group, whether absolute errors differ, or whether the prediction distributions differ. These are different properties.
It may also ask whether prediction intervals contain future outcomes often enough. That concerns uncertainty coverage. An interval can improve coverage while leaving the point prediction completely unchanged.
crumbs: 10  Post-hoc methods: regression and uncertainty intervals

title: 10  Post-hoc methods: regression and uncertainty intervals
text:
10.2 Quantile transport
Let \(F_a\) be the distribution function of predicted values in group \(a\), and \(F_a^{-1}\) its quantile function. A person’s percentile within their group is \(F_a(s)\). A transport map replaces that score with the same percentile in a reference distribution.
For squared Wasserstein distance in one dimension,
\[
W_2^2(F_a,F_b)=\int_0^1\{F_a^{-1}(u)-F_b^{-1}(u)\}^2\,du.
\]
Given nonnegative reference masses \(\pi_b\) summing to one, the Wasserstein barycenter has quantile function
\[
Q_B(u)=\sum_b\pi_b F_b^{-1}(u).
\]
The full repair is
\[
g(s,a)=Q_B\{F_a(s)\}.
\tag{10.1}\]
Under the continuous-distribution construction, this maps each group’s predictions to the same distribution. The squared-loss interpretation and optimality results in fair regression depend on the source paper’s assumptions (Chzhen et al. 2020).
In words. If a prediction is at the 70th percentile of its group’s predictions, move it to the 70th percentile of the chosen common distribution. The reference masses are part of the policy; equal group weighting and population weighting need not produce the same map.
The map can be fitted from scores and group membership without outcomes. Outcomes are still needed to evaluate errors or select a useful strength of repair. Applying the map needs group membership.
crumbs: 10  Post-hoc methods: regression and uncertainty intervals

title: 10  Post-hoc methods: regression and uncertainty intervals
text:
10.3 Partial repair
Full distributional parity may make an unacceptable change. Under the squared-Wasserstein convention used in the CFT paper, partial repair is
\[
g_\alpha(s,a)=\sqrt\alpha\,s+(1-\sqrt\alpha)g(s,a),
\qquad 0\le\alpha\le1.
\tag{10.2}\]
Here \(\alpha=0\) gives full repair and \(\alpha=1\) leaves the score unchanged. At \(\alpha=0.25\), the two predictions receive equal weight. Other implementations may parameterise interpolation differently, so always state the formula (Chzhen and Schreuder 2022).
The parameter controls this particular distributional change. It does not request a specified MAE difference or clinical benefit.
CFT scope. The native implementation estimates distributions on calibration predictions, with declared weights where supported. Deterministic mid-ranks handle ties, and endpoint quantiles handle scores outside calibration support. These choices matter for zero-heavy spending and tails. They do not inherit every continuous or jitter-based guarantee in the source literature (McCarthy 2026).
crumbs: 10  Post-hoc methods: regression and uncertainty intervals

title: 10  Post-hoc methods: regression and uncertainty intervals
text:
10.4 Clinical interpretation of distributional repair
Imagine a service using predicted expenditure to plan a budget. Equal prediction distributions might conflict with genuine differences in expected spending. If the same score is used as a proxy for unmet need, equalising expenditure predictions still may not correct the proxy problem.
Review signed error, MAE or RMSE, upper-tail errors, ranks, and downstream allocation. A transport map can be mathematically successful and clinically unhelpful. The long paper illustrates this with different patterns across diabetes progression and MEPS expenditure; it does not identify a universally preferred repair (McCarthy 2026).

Show two group prediction distributions and their common quantile reference. Trace the same within-group percentile to the common value. Add a partial-repair slider sketch. Label the target as prediction-distribution parity, not equal clinical need or equal error.

title: 10  Post-hoc methods: regression and uncertainty intervals
text:
10.5 Group split-conformal intervals
Conformal methods use a separate calibration sample to turn prediction errors into uncertainty sets. For a frozen point predictor \(f\) and group \(a\), define absolute calibration residuals
\[
r_i=|Y_i-f(X_i)|,\qquad i\in\mathcal D_{\mathrm{cal},a}.
\]
With \(n_a\) calibration observations and target miscoverage \(\eta\), use the order statistic
\[
k_a=\left\lceil(n_a+1)(1-\eta)\right\rceil,\qquad
I_a(x)=[f(x)-r_{a,(k_a)},\ f(x)+r_{a,(k_a)}].
\tag{10.3}\]
If \(k_a>n_a\), take the radius as infinite. Replacing it with the largest finite residual would silently weaken the stated finite-sample construction.
Under exchangeability within the declared group, with the fitting/calibration separation required by the method, this construction gives
\[
P\{Y_{\mathrm{new}}\in I_a(X_{\mathrm{new}})\mid A_{\mathrm{new}}=a\}\ge1-\eta.
\]
This is a group-conditional marginal statement over the calibration sample and new observation. It is not a guarantee for each individual, each covariate value, or every realised calibration sample. It also does not promise equal interval widths (Romano et al. 2020).
crumbs: 10  Post-hoc methods: regression and uncertainty intervals

title: 10  Post-hoc methods: regression and uncertainty intervals
text:
10.6 A small conformal example
Suppose there are 19 calibration residuals in a group and the target coverage is 90%. Then \(k=\lceil20\times0.9\rceil=18\). If the 18th residual is 12 units, the interval around a prediction of 50 is \([38,62]\).
With only four residuals, \(k=\lceil5\times0.9\rceil=5\). There is no fifth observed residual, so the stated construction requires an unbounded interval. These invented values illustrate why nominal coverage and practical usefulness must be reported together.
An interval that is wide enough to include almost every plausible outcome may be statistically conservative but unhelpful for a clinical decision. Compare coverage, width, and how those vary across groups and outcome ranges.
crumbs: 10  Post-hoc methods: regression and uncertainty intervals

title: 10  Post-hoc methods: regression and uncertainty intervals
text:
10.7 What changes in real datasets?
The CFT implementation uses symmetric absolute-residual intervals. Romano and colleagues’ equalized-coverage work includes more flexible quantile-based constructions. The simple adapter should not be described as a reproduction of every method in that paper.
Repeated observations require a unit-specific contract. Using a maximum residual per cluster/group changes the target to simultaneous coverage for that group’s members of a new exchangeable cluster. It is not the same as individual-row coverage.
Arbitrary survey weights do not by themselves establish weighted conformal validity. A sampling or likelihood-ratio argument is required. The current CFT adapter rejects unsupported nonuniform weighting rather than quietly discarding it. Distribution shift can also break exchangeability; a 90% label is not a permanent property of the interval (McCarthy 2026).

Illustration placeholder — Coverage and width together.
Show future outcomes as dots against intervals in two groups. Give both groups similar achieved coverage but visibly different widths. Include a sorted calibration-residual strip with the finite-sample order statistic marked. Label all values as illustrative.

text:
10.8 Questions to discuss

Does equalising prediction distributions establish equal MAE?
What is the partial-repair weight on the original score when \(\alpha=0.25\)?
What does a 90% group conformal statement say about one particular patient’s outcome?

title: 11  Post-hoc methods: survival and censoring
text:
11.1 Censoring changes both fitting and evaluation
At a chosen horizon, some patients have an observed event and some are known to remain event-free. Patients censored before that horizon have unknown event status. A binary postprocessor fitted to the raw event flag treats an observation-process variable as if it were the clinical horizon outcome.
Using a censoring-aware metric afterwards does not repair that fitting target. The postprocessor itself needs a suitable survival construction.
The output also matters. Ranking scores support some discrimination analyses, but recalibrating a horizon probability or a survival curve needs actual probabilities or curves with a stated time origin and units.
crumbs: 11  Post-hoc methods: survival and censoring

title: 11  Post-hoc methods: survival and censoring
text:
11.2 A censoring-aware loss
Let \(r_i(\tau)\) be predicted event risk by horizon \(\tau\). Let \(G\) be the censoring survival function, estimated from an appropriate reference sample. One IPCW Brier construction is
\[
\widehat R_\tau=\frac1n\sum_i\left[
\frac{\delta_i\mathbf{1}\{U_i\le\tau\}}{\widehat G(U_i^-)}
\{1-r_i(\tau)\}^2
+\frac{\mathbf{1}\{U_i>\tau\}}{\widehat G(\tau)}r_i(\tau)^2
\right].
\tag{11.1}\]
The first term scores observed events by the horizon; the second scores patients observed beyond it. Patients censored earlier contribute neither observed binary label. Weighting compensates for observation under the required assumptions (Graf et al. 1999).
The displayed left limit states a tie convention; implementations should use a consistent convention with their estimator. Positive censoring support is necessary but not sufficient. A pooled \(G\) requires an appropriate independence assumption. If observation depends on group or covariates in a relevant way, a conditional or stratified censoring model may be needed.
Large weights near the end of follow-up can make estimates unstable. Report support by group and horizon, and do not make an unsupported late horizon appear reliable by extrapolating without an explicit model.

Illustration placeholder — Known and unknown at day 90.
Draw three patient timelines: event at day 40, event-free observation to day 120, and censoring at day 40. Mark the 90-day horizon. Label the third outcome “unknown at day 90”, never “no event”.

title: 11  Post-hoc methods: survival and censoring
text:
11.3 Pseudo-observation multicalibration
Pseudo-observations provide a way to construct patient-level targets from a survival estimator. Within calibration stratum \(b\) of size \(n_b\), an event-risk pseudo-observation at horizon \(\tau\) is
\[
\widetilde Y_i(\tau)=n_b\widehat F_b^{\mathrm{KM}}(\tau)
-(n_b-1)\widehat F_{b,-i}^{\mathrm{KM}}(\tau),
\tag{11.2}\]
where \(\widehat F^{\mathrm{KM}}=1-\widehat S^{\mathrm{KM}}\) and the second estimate omits patient \(i\). This is a jackknife quantity, not an observed individual outcome. It can lie outside \([0,1]\) (Andersen and Pohar Perme 2010).
For a finite family of eligible group/bin indicators \(h\), a calibration target is
\[
\max_{h\in\mathcal H}
\left|\frac{\sum_i h_i\{\widetilde Y_i(\tau)-r_i(\tau)\}}
{\sum_i h_i}\right|\le\epsilon.
\]
An illustrative update adds the selected cell’s residual mean \(\Delta_h\) to its current risks:
\[
r_i^{(m+1)}(\tau)=\operatorname{clip}_{[0,1]}
\{r_i^{(m)}(\tau)+h_i\Delta_h^{(m)}\}.
\]
Ye and Li develop a broader multicalibration approach for censored survival (Ye and Li 2025). The CFT implementation is a restricted finite-auditor adaptation using primary groups and bins of original scores. A sufficient assumption for its plain stratum-specific KM construction is independence of censoring from event time and calibration covariates within the stratum, together with horizon support. Merely supplying a stratum label does not establish this.
Separate horizon updates can produce incoherent curves. CFT repairs the time ordering and checks residual errors after repair, since repairing monotonicity can change calibration. Meeting a finite calibration-cell target is not universal protection for arbitrary intersections or future populations (McCarthy 2026).
crumbs: 11  Post-hoc methods: survival and censoring

title: 11  Post-hoc methods: survival and censoring
text:
11.4 Conformalized survival distributions
Conformalized survival distributions (CSD) adjust predicted event-time quantiles using held-out survival outcomes (Qi et al. 2024). Let \(Q_i(v)\) be the source event-time quantile at CDF level \(v\).
In the CFT paper’s KM-sampling adaptation, observed events retain their times. For a censored patient, simulated times are drawn from an estimated event-time distribution conditional on survival past the censoring time:
\[
T_i^{(m)}\sim\widehat F_{\mathrm{ref}}(\cdot\mid T>U_i),\qquad
R_{im}(v)=Q_i(v)-T_i^{(m)}.
\]
This \(F_{\mathrm{ref}}\) concerns event times. It is different from the censoring distribution \(G\) used in Equation 11.1. Simulated values are assumptions-based draws, not recovered patient outcomes.
For \(n\) calibration patients, the documented correction is
\[
b_v=\min\left\{\frac{\lceil(n+1)(1-v)\rceil}{n},1\right\},\quad
c_v=\widehat Q_{b_v}\{R_{im}(v)\},\quad
Q_i^*(v)=Q_i(v)-c_v.
\tag{11.3}\]
Simulation draws do not increase the independent patient count in the correction. The adjusted quantiles require positivity and ordering before conversion into curves. Unsupported tail quantiles need an explicit extrapolation assumption or an incompatible result.
CSD targets distribution calibration, not a protected-group parity constraint. Censoring assumptions, reference fit, simulation, and quantile repair affect the native adaptation. The source paper’s theoretical results should not be restated as an unconditional guarantee for this finite implementation or for every horizon-specific metric (McCarthy 2026).
crumbs: 11  Post-hoc methods: survival and censoring

title: 11  Post-hoc methods: survival and censoring
text:
11.5 Sensitive-input curve averaging
EquiSurv motivates averaging source-model curves over alternative sensitive-input values (Zhao and Ng 2023). For prespecified weights \(\pi_b\),
\[
\overline S(t\mid x)=\sum_b\pi_b S_{\mathrm{src}}(t\mid x,A=b),
\qquad \pi_b\ge0,\quad\sum_b\pi_b=1.
\tag{11.4}\]
A convex mixture preserves valid survival-curve shape. At the fixed other inputs \(x\), the averaged result no longer depends on the patient’s supplied observed value of \(A\).
However, other inputs can differ between groups and can carry consequences of structural conditions. Input-replacement invariance therefore does not imply equal group outcomes, equal errors, or a causally identified counterfactual effect.
One observed curve per person is insufficient. The source model must support the alternative-input evaluations, and those evaluations must be meaningful. If \(A\) is already excluded and has no effect on the source prediction, averaging its replacements produces no substantive intervention.
CFT scope. An explicit external curve bundle supplies the alternative-input curves, row identities, time definitions, and source provenance. Compare the average against the same source model under observed inputs. An unrelated baseline would mix the effect of averaging with the effect of changing models (McCarthy 2026).
crumbs: 11  Post-hoc methods: survival and censoring

title: 11  Post-hoc methods: survival and censoring
text:
11.6 What an acceptable comparison retains
Keep the original curve, adjusted curve, fitting horizon, evaluation horizons, group support, and censoring assumptions. Assess calibration, discrimination, and clinically relevant decisions after the complete adjustment. If curves cross or require tail repair, report that behaviour.
A calibration gain on development data can disappear on evaluation data. The long CFT paper includes examples where native survival adjustments worsen evaluation measures. Those results are evidence about the implemented settings and cohorts, not a general verdict on every version of the underlying research method (McCarthy 2026).

Which distribution describes censoring in IPCW, and which describes event times in CSD sampling?

title: 12  Other fairness methods and research directions
text:
12.1 The problem may start before prediction
Post-processing is useful when a model is already fitted, but it cannot address every source of harm. A target that measures access rather than need may require a new endpoint. A population absent from development data may require recruitment. A device that measures differently across patients may require measurement work.
This chapter is a research overview beyond the handbook’s CFT post-hoc workflows. It does not claim that CFT implements fairness-aware training or causal identification. The examples remain compatible with classical statistical and ML models; deep learning is not required.
crumbs: 12  Other fairness methods and research directions

title: 12  Other fairness methods and research directions
text:
12.2 Data collection and preprocessing
Improving representation can mean collecting data from missing settings, languages, or patient groups. It can also mean improving outcome follow-up or measurement consistency. More rows from the same narrow population may not solve the original coverage problem.
Reweighting changes each observation’s contribution to a fitting objective:
\[
\widehat R_w(f)=\frac{\sum_i w_i\ell\{Y_i,f(X_i)\}}{\sum_iw_i}.
\]
The meaning depends on the weights. Survey weights represent a sampling design. Transport weights aim to represent another population. Fairness-motivated weights change the optimisation emphasis. These uses should not be interchanged without justification.
Resampling can change class or group balance, but duplicating rare records does not create independent information. Synthetic examples can also reproduce unwanted correlations or create implausible combinations. Evaluate representation and measurement quality alongside predictive results (Suresh and Guttag 2021).
crumbs: 12  Other fairness methods and research directions

title: 12  Other fairness methods and research directions
text:
12.3 Penalties and constraints during learning
A fairness penalty combines predictive loss and a disparity term:
\[
\widehat f=\arg\min_f\{\widehat R(f)+\lambda\widehat\Phi(f)\}.
\]
The parameter \(\lambda\) controls an optimisation trade-off, not a clinical preference by itself. The disparity \(\Phi\) needs a definition, supported denominators, and a link to the intended action.
A constrained version is
\[
\min_f\widehat R(f)\quad\text{subject to}\quad
\widehat\Phi_j(f)\le\epsilon_j.
\]
These approaches require training access and development-only selection. Constraints measured during training do not automatically hold in another population. Clinical empirical work shows why calibration, ranking, and utility should still be evaluated after targeting parity (Pfohl et al. 2021).
crumbs: 12  Other fairness methods and research directions

title: 12  Other fairness methods and research directions
text:
12.4 Reductions and robust objectives
Reductions solve a fairness-constrained problem through a sequence of cost-sensitive learning problems. They can reuse a compatible base learner and produce a mixture of classifiers. This is a training procedure, unlike choosing a threshold for one frozen predictor (Agarwal et al. 2018, 2019).
Distributionally robust optimisation can target the worst expected loss over a specified set of plausible distributions:
\[
\min_f\sup_{P\in\mathcal U}E_P[\ell\{Y,f(X)\}].
\]
The uncertainty set \(\mathcal U\) determines what “worst” means. It might emphasise certain groups or distributions near the observed data. A group absent from the data does not gain reliable protection simply because the objective is called robust. Survival losses add risk-set and dependence issues that need survival-specific treatment (Hu and Chen 2024).
crumbs: 12  Other fairness methods and research directions

title: 12  Other fairness methods and research directions
text:
12.5 Causal and counterfactual fairness
An input sensitivity check asks what the fitted model returns when a column is changed while other inputs remain fixed. This can expose direct model dependence. It does not establish what would happen to a person in another causal world.
Kusner and colleagues define counterfactual fairness through a structural causal model. A simplified statement is
\[
P(\widehat Y_{A\leftarrow a}(U)=y\mid X=x,A=a)
=P(\widehat Y_{A\leftarrow a'}(U)=y\mid X=x,A=a)
\]
for alternative values \(a'\) and relevant outcomes \(y\). Here \(U\) denotes background factors in the causal model, and the subscript denotes an intervention within that model (Kusner et al. 2017).
The difficult work is specifying credible pathways, deciding which pathways are relevant to fairness, and establishing what the data can identify. Race and gender are socially and historically situated; a formal intervention on a variable is not automatically a coherent real-world intervention on a person’s identity.
For example, holding access-dependent laboratory measurements fixed while changing a demographic field does not represent all the pathways through which unequal access shaped the record. Conversely, allowing every downstream variable to change requires causal assumptions that an ordinary prediction table cannot supply.

Illustration placeholder — A column edit and a causal question.
Use two panels. The first shows an input field edited while other columns stay fixed. The second shows a proposed causal diagram in which structural conditions affect access, measurements, and outcomes. Mark assumptions as assumptions and avoid presenting demographic categories as simple biological causes.

title: 12  Other fairness methods and research directions
section: 12.6 Fairness may require a service change
text:
12.6 Fairness may require a service change
A review pathway can be improved by adding interpreter access, reducing waiting time, or making follow-up reachable. Better outcome ascertainment can expose a disparity that was previously hidden. Changing the model may be only one part of a response.
These changes also need evaluation. Increased referrals are useful only if the service can deliver the intended benefit without shifting unacceptable burdens onto patients or staff. Patient participation helps identify what counts as a meaningful improvement.

title: 13  Worked cases: reading the whole result
text:
13.1 Case 1: the smaller gap that misses more patients
All numbers in this chapter are invented teaching examples. They are not CFT benchmark results. The accompanying manuscript lessons are qualitative and cited separately.
A service considers a readmission alert for additional discharge support. There are 100 observed cases in each group.
The gap disappears, but detected cases fall from 140 to 20 out of 200. The adjusted policy misses 180 cases. Calling this an improvement based only on EOpp would conceal the most obvious clinical consequence.
The long CFT paper uses a real readmission comparison to make the same type of argument: a binary gap can become small alongside very low sensitivity. The values above are simplified for teaching and are not transcribed from that study (McCarthy 2026).
A useful interpretation: “Sensitivity is equal in the proposed policy, but low in both groups and substantially lower than baseline. The policy does not satisfy the service’s intended detection purpose. False-positive burden and capacity also need review.”
The next step is to revisit the development objective and operating constraints, not select another threshold using the evaluation cohort and call it independently validated.

title: 13  Worked cases: reading the whole result
text:
13.2 Case 2: the missing subgroup denominator
A diagnostic evaluation contains 400 patients in one group, but no observed examples of a rare diagnostic category. The report leaves class-specific sensitivity blank for that group.
This is appropriate. There are no observed true cases from which to estimate detection. Entering zero would mean the model detected none of some known cases, which is a different statement. Entering 100% would be equally misleading.
A useful interpretation: “Detection of this category cannot be estimated in this group because the evaluation cohort contains no observed cases. The overall multiclass summary does not resolve this missing evidence.”
The next step might be targeted data collection or a narrower claim. Removing the group from the headline gap without explaining why makes the audit look more complete than it is.
