title: 13  Worked cases: reading the whole result
section: 13.3 Case 3: an accurate spending model with the wrong use
text:
13.3 Case 3: an accurate spending model with the wrong use
A spending model predicts annual expenditure reasonably well across groups. A service proposes using it to identify people with the greatest unmet need.
The target has changed. Expected spending reflects illness, access, service availability, and historical treatment. Good expenditure prediction does not establish good prediction of unmet need. Distributional repair of spending scores cannot by itself establish that the resulting allocation matches need (Obermeyer et al. 2019).
Suppose a transport method reduces the difference between average predictions from 500 currency units to 50, while MAE rises from 300 to 450. This is a measurable distributional change, but neither number tells us whether the right patients receive support.
A useful interpretation: “The adjustment changes spending predictions and increases absolute error in this example. Before evaluating allocation fairness, the service needs a justified measure of clinical need or expected benefit and evidence about the proposed support.”
The long paper’s diabetes and MEPS examples also show that regression transport can have different error effects in different datasets. A favourable result in one task does not settle its suitability for another (McCarthy 2026).

section: 13.5 Case 5: the patient censored before the horizon
text:
13.5 Case 5: the patient censored before the horizon
Three patients receive a 90-day prognosis. One has the event at day 30. One is followed without the event to day 120. One is last seen without the event at day 40.
Only the first two have known 90-day status. The third cannot be treated as a known non-case. If early loss to follow-up is more common in one group, a naive binary audit can reflect follow-up differences as well as event risk.
A useful interpretation: “The horizon analysis requires a censoring-aware estimator and adequate support. We need to justify the censoring model and investigate group differences in follow-up before interpreting a disparity as a model-performance difference.”
The long CFT paper retains this boundary in its survival methods and notes limitations of pooled censoring references. Finite-sample numerical checks do not establish the underlying independence assumptions (McCarthy 2026).

title: 13  Worked cases: reading the whole result
text:
13.6 Case 6: deferral moves the work
Before deferral, a model is 85% accurate across 1,000 patients. After deferral, it is 95% accurate among 600 retained patients. The 400 deferred patients are not included in that accuracy calculation.
If one group is deferred much more often, it may face extra appointments or delays. Without reviewer outcomes, the combined system’s accuracy and clinical benefit are unknown.
A useful interpretation: “Retained accuracy improved while automation coverage fell to 60%. We need group-specific coverage, reasons for deferral, reviewer capacity, waiting times, and downstream outcomes to assess the complete pathway.”
This illustrates why CFT retained-set metrics should remain explicitly conditional (McCarthy 2026).

13.7 A reusable reading sequence
For each case, read the population and task first, then the unchanged baseline. Identify what the intervention changes, examine the group rates and denominators, assess utility and uncertainty, and finally state what remains unknown.
The strongest next step is not always another algorithm. It may be to revise the outcome, collect missing evidence, improve service access, or decide that the proposed model use is unsupported.

title: 14  Using the Clinical Fairness Toolkit
text:
14.1 Start from the evidence you have
CFT supports several starting points. An existing model can be evaluated with suitable data and its expected preprocessing. A prediction table can be audited without loading the original model. A dataset can be used to train an illustrative baseline. A descriptive audit can examine representation and outcomes without predictions (McCarthy 2026).
The handbook records the inspected software snapshot in Appendix E. Commands and capability details can change. A named research method in this book is not permission to substitute an unsupported implementation in a particular installed version.
A partial report can be the correct output. Calculating fewer metrics honestly is more useful than manufacturing a probability from a class label or treating a rank score as a risk.

14.2 Prepare the roles explicitly
Identify the outcome, positive class or class order, predictors, audit fields, identifiers, weights, and any grouping unit. For survival, add event coding, time origin, duration units, and horizons.
For an existing model, supply the preprocessing it expects. The audit does not reconstruct an unknown development history. Declare evaluation and calibration cohorts and check known identifier overlap, while recognising that absent identifiers limit what can be verified.
A group-aware postprocessor needs its inputs at deployment as well as fitting. A CSV containing only one score per patient cannot support an intervention that needs alternative-input model evaluations.

text:
14.3 A reproducible starting workflow
The commands below are examples to run from the toolkit repository, using the cft environment. They are not executed when rendering this book and may need dataset preparation before the report can run.
# Validate a prepared audit configuration before fitting or evaluation.
python -m cft.cli validate-config audit.yaml --execution

# Run the declared report.
python -m cft.cli report --config audit.yaml

# Request the optional PDF export of the same report.
python -m cft.cli report --config audit.yaml --pdf

# Open the clinical workspace.
python -m streamlit run src/cft/demo/app.py
On the author’s Windows workspace, the environment’s interpreter is C:/Users/Nick/anaconda3/envs/cft/python.exe. Other installations should use their configured CFT environment.
To explore the published examples, inspect the task and comparison configurations before running them. Some example files explicitly request interventions. Start with a declared baseline for your own question and request only methods whose task and input contracts you can satisfy. Do not infer the contents of a saved configuration from the word “default”.

section: 14.4 What to read in the report
text:
14.4 What to read in the report
First inspect the cohort and resolved configuration. Check eligibility, exclusions, group coding, outcome timing, class order, and the object being evaluated. Then read overall and subgroup performance, including support and missing metrics.
For each intervention, identify whether it changes scores, decisions, intervals, curves, or the retained cohort. Compare like with like. An interval procedure should be judged by coverage and width alongside the unchanged point prediction. A decision-only policy should not be credited with changing source-score calibration.
Finally read warnings and method states. They are part of the evidence, not decorative diagnostics.

An incompatible intervention must not be displayed as a successful baseline under another name. A smaller collection of executed methods should also not hide how many requested methods were unsupported.

14.5 Preserve a reviewable record
Retain the configuration, input provenance, split definitions, seeds, software version, method parameters, report, machine-readable evidence, and reasons for omissions. Keep supplied context and attestations distinguishable from calculated results.
This matters especially when sharing a screenshot or summary table. Without the cohort, threshold, positive class, and group definitions, an apparently simple sensitivity gap is difficult to interpret or reproduce.
The retained binary research engine and historical broad benchmarks are separate from native task-aware clinical audits. Historical results should keep their original labels and cohort scope. The handbook does not relabel them as evidence from the current clinical suite.

title: 15  Reporting, review, and monitoring
text:
15.1 Make a claim that can be checked
“The model is fair” leaves too much unspecified. A more useful statement names the population, period, outcome, policy, groups, rates, support, and uncertainty.
For example:
This is a statement a reviewer can assess. It keeps the measured property separate from the wider decision about whether the policy should be used.

title: 15  Reporting, review, and monitoring
text: In the stated evaluation cohort, at the prespecified referral threshold, sensitivity for the recorded 30-day outcome differed across the declared groups by the reported amount. The report gives group event counts and uncertainty. It does not establish equal treatment benefit or outcomes following referral.

title: 15  Reporting, review, and monitoring
section: 15.2 Assemble the evidence in a useful order
text:
15.2 Assemble the evidence in a useful order
Begin with intended use and the action. Describe the cohort, target, timing, and measurement process. Explain the model and policy, including any postprocessor. Report overall performance, group estimates, support, and uncertainty. Then describe limitations, alternatives, and the decision being requested.
TRIPOD+AI can structure prediction-model reporting; PROBAST+AI supports appraisal of quality, bias risk, and applicability. FUTURE-AI addresses the broader lifecycle. Early clinical evaluation and trials have additional reporting frameworks, including DECIDE-AI and CONSORT-AI (Collins et al. 2024; Moons et al. 2025; Lekadir et al. 2025; Vasey et al. 2022; Liu et al. 2020). A completed checklist helps organise evidence; it does not automatically approve a model or establish compliance.
The handbook does not give jurisdiction-specific legal advice or claim a regulatory status for CFT. Any intended deployment needs the relevant local review, with the actual system and proposed change clearly described.

title: 15  Reporting, review, and monitoring
section: 15.3 The path from retrospective results to use
text:
15.3 The path from retrospective results to use
Internal evaluation tells us how a procedure behaved in the studied data. External or temporal evaluation examines transfer to another site or period. Prospective evaluation can reveal whether inputs arrive on time, whether staff understand outputs, and whether the intended pathway occurs.
A change in patient outcomes requires evidence about use of the system. That may call for a comparative clinical study appropriate to the intervention. A retrospective threshold comparison alone does not observe clinician responses, patient uptake, treatment effects, or delays.
The long CFT paper explicitly treats its comparisons as exploratory internal evidence. Untuned models, repeated use of source cohorts, incomplete uncertainty, and adaptation-specific assumptions limit what can be claimed (McCarthy 2026). These limits should travel with teaching examples drawn from the paper.

title: 15  Reporting, review, and monitoring
section: 15.4 Monitor the pathway, not just the score
text:
15.4 Monitor the pathway, not just the score
After implementation, the population, measurement process, and service can change. A model may remain numerically stable while access to the recommended action deteriorates.

Monitoring needs a denominator and a time window. Separate patients whose outcome is not yet mature from those with a known negative outcome. A sudden apparent improvement can come from shorter follow-up or missing labels.

title: 15  Reporting, review, and monitoring
section: 15.5 Agree what happens when evidence changes
text:
15.5 Agree what happens when evidence changes
Assign an owner for data quality, model performance, and the clinical pathway. Agree what signals require investigation, additional data, a pause, or a model or policy update. Thresholds for action should reflect clinical consequences and the precision of the estimates, rather than an arbitrary parity cutoff.
An update creates a new procedure to evaluate. Recalibration can change decisions; a threshold update can alter workload; a new group definition can change who is covered. Retain versioned records and compare the changed system with a relevant baseline.
Repeated monitoring also creates repeated opportunities for noisy alerts. Use a justified monitoring method and distinguish a signal requiring review from a confirmed deterioration. Record unresolved evidence rather than smoothing it away.

title: 15  Reporting, review, and monitoring
text:
15.6 Participation and accountability
Patients and staff should be able to understand the role of the model, raise concerns, and obtain review through an appropriate pathway. Ask whose experience is absent from the dataset and whose burden is absent from the metric.
An audit team should be able to say what evidence would change its mind. A useful report supports a concrete next decision: gather more data, change the endpoint, investigate a subgroup, revise a policy, evaluate prospectively, or decline the proposed use.

Illustration placeholder — Evidence returning to the team.
Show a loop from model and policy versions to decisions, access, outcomes, subgroup review, and a documented response. Put delayed labels and patient feedback on separate incoming paths. Keep the human decision to update visible.

C.1 Introduction and background
These are discussion guides. A defensible answer should explain its population, assumptions, and clinical use.

title: Appendix C — Suggested answers to chapter questions
text:
Similar accuracy describes recorded patients and their predictions. It does not measure unequal access to the service or people absent from the dataset.
Evidence is needed about the changed action, uptake, benefits, burdens, and patient outcomes. A narrower statistical gap alone does not establish this.
crumbs: C  Suggested answers to chapter questions

title: Appendix C — Suggested answers to chapter questions
text:
C.2 Clinical applications

When prevalence is very low, most negative results may be correct even if many of the few cases are missed. Sensitivity uses actual cases as its denominator; NPV uses negative decisions.
Specify how limited appointments are allocated, how queues work, and what happens to people who cannot be served. Evaluate the resulting complete policy.
Risk concerns an outcome under the observed or modelled conditions. Benefit concerns the difference caused by an action. They need different evidence.
crumbs: C  Suggested answers to chapter questions

title: Appendix C — Suggested answers to chapter questions
text:
C.3 Data and audit design

Whole-dataset preprocessing uses information from evaluation data when constructing the fitted procedure, which can make evaluation optimistic or unlike the intended deployment process.
The audit describes the included population with supported recorded group values. The number and characteristics of excluded patients, and the limitation this creates, should be reported.
Establish whether spending represents the intended need or treatment benefit. Review access and measurement pathways rather than inferring suitability from predictive accuracy.
crumbs: C  Suggested answers to chapter questions

title: Appendix C — Suggested answers to chapter questions
text:
C.4 Modelling approaches

Dichotomisation discards magnitude and introduces an additional threshold. Different cutoffs can produce different clinical questions and fairness results.
A Cox linear predictor describes a relative hazard ordering. A horizon probability also needs baseline survival, time units, and a time origin.
Independent thresholds can select multiple categories or none. A mutually exclusive outcome needs one joint rule.
crumbs: C  Suggested answers to chapter questions

title: Appendix C — Suggested answers to chapter questions
text:
C.5 Utility

A constant probability can be calibrated at the cohort level while failing to distinguish patients with different risks. Calibration does not guarantee useful discrimination.
Positive and negative errors can cancel. Compare absolute error, squared error, distributions, and relevant tails.
AUROC does not specify the threshold, workload, clinical consequences, or value of action. The policy requires decision-specific evaluation.
crumbs: C  Suggested answers to chapter questions

title: Appendix C — Suggested answers to chapter questions
text:
C.6 Fairness

No. Equal sensitivity can be equally low. Report both rates and counts and assess whether detection is useful.
Prevalence differs. With equal TPR and FPR, Bayes’ rule still produces different PPV.
There is no defined positive outcome, TPR, or FPR. A meaningful continuous-outcome criterion or a justified threshold-specific event must be stated.
crumbs: C  Suggested answers to chapter questions

title: Appendix C — Suggested answers to chapter questions
text:
C.7 Uncertainty

PPV’s denominator is the number of positive decisions, not total patients or total observed cases.
It preserves within-patient dependence by resampling the independent unit. A row bootstrap treats correlated encounters as independent information.
It generally leaves out training and selection variation, measurement bias, unrepresented populations, and future shift unless the design explicitly models them.
crumbs: C  Suggested answers to chapter questions

title: Appendix C — Suggested answers to chapter questions
text:
C.8 Binary post-processing

The source scores and their ordering are unchanged; only the decisions differ. Report score and decision metrics as distinct objects.
It introduces an action probability and sampling variation. Reproducibility, repeated encounters, and clinical acceptability need explicit policies.
Measure group coverage, reviewer capacity, delay, subsequent decisions, and outcomes for deferred patients. Retained performance alone omits that pathway.
crumbs: C  Suggested answers to chapter questions

title: Appendix C — Suggested answers to chapter questions
text:
C.9 Multiclass post-processing

Each row is a conditional probability distribution over the one class that will be output.
Argmax changes expected action frequencies and conditional rates. A constraint fitted for \(q\) need not hold for its largest-probability class.
Include an unadjusted policy that samples from the original probabilities, alongside the original argmax baseline and adjusted policy.
crumbs: C  Suggested answers to chapter questions

title: Appendix C — Suggested answers to chapter questions
text:
C.10 Regression post-processing

No. Prediction-distribution parity makes no general statement about the relationship between predictions and each group’s outcomes.
\(\sqrt{0.25}=0.5\), so the original and fully transported predictions receive equal weight.
It provides no guarantee for a particular fixed patient. The stated result is marginal over calibration and future observations within the declared group under exchangeability.
crumbs: C  Suggested answers to chapter questions

title: Appendix C — Suggested answers to chapter questions
text:
C.11 Survival post-processing

The raw flag records whether an event was observed during available follow-up. A person censored early has unknown status at the chosen horizon.
\(G\) describes the censoring distribution for IPCW; \(F_{\mathrm{ref}}\) describes event times for the CSD sampling approximation.
It fixes other observed covariates and averages model evaluations. It does not identify all causal pathways or remove group differences in those covariates.

title: Appendix C — Suggested answers to chapter questions
text:
C.12 Other methods

Survey weights support inference for a sampling population. Fairness weights alter an optimisation objective. Their assumptions and intended quantities differ.
It does not specify acceptable false positives, missed cases, workload, or patient burden, and its numerical scale depends on the losses.
A structural causal model, meaningful interventions, assumptions about pathways and background factors, and an identification argument are needed.

text:
C.13 Worked cases

“The EOpp gap fell from 20 percentage points to zero, while detected cases fell from 140 to 20 out of 200. Sensitivity is now 10% in both groups.”
Evidence for all patients, including group-specific retention, reviewer actions and accuracy, waits, burdens, and subsequent outcomes.

title: Appendix C — Suggested answers to chapter questions
text:
C.14 Using CFT

Supported confusion-based metrics and decision fairness comparisons remain possible. Probability calibration and ranking claims need appropriate scores.
It means the computation completed. Clinical assumptions, applicability, and consequences are separate questions.
Population and dates, endpoint and horizon, group definitions, threshold or policy, denominators, uncertainty, provenance, and relevant omissions.

title: Appendix C — Suggested answers to chapter questions
text:
C.15 Reporting and monitoring

Clinician response, patient uptake, access, treatment effects, waits, and downstream outcomes may all remain unobserved.
Patients with unobserved events may be incorrectly counted as non-cases, or the evaluated cohort may become selectively observed.
Examples include worsened calibration, new missingness, increased false-positive burden, unequal waiting times, more deferral, or loss of outcome follow-up.

title: Appendix D — Illustration briefs
text:
D.1 Priority concepts
The book currently uses textual placeholders. These briefs specify original diagrams to commission or generate later. They do not require copying figures from the papers. Every eventual figure should have a visible caption, alternative text, a source or creation record, and a clear distinction between schematic and empirical content.
Calibration. Use directly labelled axes and an ideal diagonal. Show counts or a density strip so empty score regions are not presented as established evidence. If a pooled curve hides group errors, construct the example numerically rather than drawing an unsupported pattern.
Conformal prediction. A sorted residual strip is often clearer than a decorative confidence band. Display the finite-sample order statistic and distinguish a future-outcome interval from a confidence interval for a mean. Equal coverage should coexist visibly with potentially unequal widths.
Counterfactuals. Use a two-panel explanation. A simple edit holds other columns fixed. A causal intervention is defined within an explicit model of how variables arise. Do not illustrate identity as a biological switch or claim that the causal diagram has been established from the prediction data.

title: Appendix D — Illustration briefs
text:
D.2 Visual language
Use a restrained teal, blue, and warm-grey palette, with direct labels, patterns, or line styles so colour is never the only cue. Avoid red/green group coding, stereotyped patient portraits, and “good” versus “bad” demographic colours. Use large, readable text and consistent notation.
Mathematical plots should be generated from checked numerical data with ordinary plotting tools. Generated artwork can support a human setting or conceptual scene, but should not be trusted to create precise axes, equations, or experimental results. Keep editable source assets with the figure record.

title: Appendix E — Source notes and scope
text:
E.1 How the manuscripts informed the book
The handbook develops arguments from the current CFT short announcement, long empirical paper, and background chapter. It is a teaching synthesis rather than a systematic review or a transcription of the papers.
The publication source snapshot is commit a5b5858fb34c2b4fd46320f9717cbf68d4efc242 in the publication repository. The toolkit snapshot inspected is commit bfb2d5fe96641bf54c641a781d6779c055a673a4 in the toolkit repository. Both were read for this edition on 5 November 2026. File hashes are retained in the handbook repository’s sources/manifest.json.
The supplied project guidance preserves baseline-first clinical boundaries and a separate retained binary research engine. The inspected toolkit additionally contains explicit native intervention contracts and opt-in comparison configurations. The handbook describes those documented adaptations without extending them or implying that every saved example is baseline-only. A future software update needs a fresh capability check.

section: E.2 Empirical findings and teaching examples
text:
E.2 Empirical findings and teaching examples
The book uses qualitative lessons from the current long paper without reproducing benchmark tables. Its worked numbers are invented and labelled. Earlier broad binary benchmarks and historical publication matrices are not presented as current task-suite results.
The papers are working manuscripts. Their experiments are internal, exploratory evidence and do not establish patient-care benefit. Method papers establish particular mathematical results under their assumptions; the handbook does not automatically transfer those results to a restricted implementation.

title: Appendix E — Source notes and scope
text:
E.3 References and checks
Bibliographic entries were drawn from the publication repository’s clinical-references.bib, restricted to works actually cited, with separate entries for the two working manuscripts. Core source locations were checked against primary publisher, proceedings, author, or official documentation pages during preparation. This is not an exhaustive new literature search or independent replication of each paper.
Examples of primary sources checked include Hardt and colleagues, Romano and colleagues, Agarwal and colleagues, Xian and colleagues, Qi and colleagues, TRIPOD+AI, and FUTURE-AI.

title: Appendix E — Source notes and scope
text:
E.4 Editorial boundaries
This edition includes illustration briefs rather than finished illustrations. It contains no borrowed figure assets, patient-level data, new model runs, clinical approvals, or invented governance attestations. The audit worksheet intentionally leaves project-specific facts blank.
Before a public textbook release, the author should review clinical wording, source interpretations, and the scope of each implementation claim; replace the illustration placeholders; and decide authorship, licensing, and publication details. These are editorial tasks, not claims that the current draft has been externally reviewed.
